Eighth grade science · Unit 8.5

Light, Waves & Information

Every video call, every streamed song, and every text message is a pattern carried by waves. Building on Unit 1: Light and Matter, Unit 7.8: The Electromagnetic Spectrum, and Unit 8.4: Sound Waves, this unit asks: how do waves bend and bounce, and how do we use them to store and send information? Collect measurements and compare them with predictions as in Unit 0: How Science Works.

Where we left off: Units 7.8 and 8.4 described light and sound as waves. You may already have learned how light reflects and is absorbed (Unit 1). Now we see how waves bend, how fiber optics trap light, and how waves carry information as digital data.

Concept 1 · Bouncing waves

Angle in equals angle out

When a wave hits a smooth surface it reflects: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal (a line perpendicular to the surface).

Light is a wave that can travel through empty space, and it moves in straight lines until it meets something. When light hits a surface, some of it bounces off, which is called reflection. The normal is an imaginary line at a right angle to the surface at the point where the light hits. The angle of incidence is the angle between the incoming ray and the normal, and the angle of reflection is the angle between the bounced ray and the normal. On a smooth surface like a mirror these angles are equal, which gives a clear image. A rough surface scatters light in many directions.

Analogy

A pool shot

A billiard ball hitting the rail at a shallow angle bounces off at the same shallow angle on the other side.

Real world

Uses of reflection

Each mirror turns the light through 90 degrees, because the angle in equals the angle out. Two turns let you see over a wall. Try the same bounces in Laser Bounce.

UseHow
PeriscopeTwo mirrors bounce light around a corner

Concept 2 · Bending waves

Waves bend when their speed changes

Light slows down in materials like water or glass and bends toward the normal when it enters them (refraction). The slower it goes (the higher the index n), the more it bends.

Light travels fastest in a vacuum, and slower in materials such as air, water and glass. Refraction is the bending of a wave when it passes from one material into another and changes speed. If light enters a slower material at an angle, it bends toward the normal (the line at right angles to the surface); going into a faster material, it bends away. The index of refraction, n, tells how much a material slows light: n = speed of light in vacuum ÷ speed in the material. Water has n of about 1.33 and glass about 1.5, so glass bends light more. Refraction makes a straw look bent in a glass of water.

Analogy

A lawn mower on grass

Think of the mower’s front axle as a wavefront. The wheel that reaches the grass first slows down, so the line of wheels swings round and the path turns toward the normal. Light entering water or glass does the same.

Push a lawn mower from pavement onto grass at an angle: one wheel slows first, so the mower turns. Light entering water does the same.

Concept 3 · Trapped light

Total internal reflection traps light in glass

If light inside glass hits the edge at a glancing enough angle (far from the perpendicular), none escapes: it reflects completely. This total internal reflection lets optical fibers carry light around bends for kilometers.

When light tries to go from a slower material (like glass or water) into a faster one (like air), it bends away from the normal. If the angle it hits the boundary is bigger than a special value called the critical angle, it cannot get out at all and is reflected back inside. This is total internal reflection. An optical fiber is a very thin strand of glass that uses it: light entering one end hits the sides at shallow angles, bounces along the whole length, and comes out the other end, even around curves, with very little loss.

Analogy

Skipping a stone

Throw a stone at a pond at a shallow angle and it skips off. Throw it straight down and it sinks. Light in a fiber is a stone that always skips.

Concept 4 · Two ways to store a wave

Smooth curves or numbers

Analog signals vary smoothly (a vinyl groove). Digital signals measure the wave at regular times (sampling) and store numbers. More samples means a closer copy, but more data. Digital copies can be copied with little degradation when errors are detected and corrected.

A signal is a pattern in a wave or a voltage that carries information, such as sound or a picture. An analog signal copies the original as a continuously changing quantity, like the wavy groove of a vinyl record. A digital signal instead measures the original at regular moments in time (sampling) and writes each measurement as a number. The more samples per second, the closer the digital copy follows the original, but the more numbers need to be stored. Analog copies pick up small errors every time they are copied or sent; digital numbers can be checked and repaired, so they travel long distances cleanly.

Analogy

A ramp and a staircase

A ramp has every height; a staircase has only certain steps. Digital sound is a staircase so fine you cannot hear the steps.

Concept 5 · Information as 0s and 1s

Waves carry binary data

A bit is a 0 or 1, like a light off or on. Eight bits make a byte, enough for one letter. Waves carry bits by changing (pulses of light, radio, or voltage) so receivers can tell 0 from 1.

Computers store and send everything as numbers made from only two symbols, 0 and 1. This two-symbol system is binary, and one 0 or 1 is a bit (short for binary digit). A group of 8 bits is a byte, which can have 256 different patterns, enough to give each letter, digit and symbol its own pattern. A code is an agreed rule that matches patterns to meanings, such as the ASCII code for text. To send bits, a wave is switched in a way both ends understand: light on or off in a fiber, a radio wave changed in strength or timing, or a voltage high or low in a wire.

Analogy

Flashlight Morse code

Flash long and short pulses to send a message across a field. Computers do the same with billions of pulses per second.

Data

First, what is binary and what is a code?

You have not met binary earlier in these lessons, so here is everything you need. A bit is one yes-or-no choice, written 0 or 1. Computers use bits because it is easy to tell two states apart, even in a noisy world: a light that is on or off, a voltage that is high or low, a tiny magnet that points north or south. Waves can carry these choices as pulses.

But letters, pictures and music are not 0s and 1s. To send them we first encode them: we agree on a code that turns each thing into a number, and then write the number in binary. A code only works if the sender and the receiver agree on it, like two friends who agree on Morse code.

  • Text. A code called ASCII gives every character a number: A is 65, B is 66, and so on up to Z. A lowercase a is 97. A space is 32. The computer stores 65 as the byte 01000001. (Modern phones use a bigger code, Unicode, which also covers other languages and emoji.)
  • Pictures. A picture is a grid of tiny squares called pixels. Each pixel's color is stored as three numbers from 0 to 255 (how much red, green and blue light).
  • Sound. As in Concept 4, a sound wave is measured many thousands of times a second, and each measurement is stored as a number.

Every one of those numbers is finally written in binary and sent as pulses of light, radio or electricity. Next you will learn how to read binary yourself.

A few codes, written in binary
ThingCode numberSent as bits
Letter A6501000001
Letter B6601000010
Letter H7201001000
Letter i (lowercase)10501101001
Space3200100000
A red pixel255, 0, 0 (red, green, blue)11111111 00000000 00000000

So the word “Hi” is sent as 01001000 01101001: two bytes, sixteen pulses of light.

Each switch has a value. Add up the values of the switches that are on. That is how a byte (8 bits) stores a number from 0 to 255.

Can you explain it?

A fiber-optic cable carries a video call from Michigan to Europe. Explain how total internal reflection keeps the light inside the cable, and why digital signals are good for long distances.

Show a model answer

Light enters the glass core and hits the core/cladding boundary at angles beyond the critical angle, so all of it reflects back in; the fiber guides the light along. A digital signal only needs the receiver to decide 0 or 1, so noise can be cleaned up and the signal regenerated, so the data arrives unchanged.

Tutor notes: hands-on kit, misconceptions, pacing

Kit (about $12): a laser pointer (adult-supervised), a small mirror, a clear tank or glass of water with a few drops of milk, a glass block or flat glass, a clear plastic bottle with a hole (laser fiber demo), graph paper, string lights, a phone camera.

  • Concept 1: Measure incident and reflected angles with a protractor.
  • Concept 2: Trace a ray through a glass block and compare it with Snell's law.
  • Concept 3: Do the laser bottle demo: light follows a curved water stream.
  • Concept 4: Draw a sound wave on graph paper and sample it at 4, 8, and 16 points.
  • Concept 5: Send a binary message with a flashlight and a decoding chart.

Common misconceptions:

  • "Light always travels in straight lines." In uniform material, yes; it bends at boundaries.
  • "Mirrors reverse left and right." They reverse front and back.
  • "Digital is always better." It is just more convenient to copy and fix.
  • "Fiber carries electricity." It carries light.

Pacing: about five 30-minute sessions. Method link: use measurements, not just pictures: predict each angle, measure, compare, and compute the error (Unit 0). Never shine a laser in anyone's eyes.

After the lesson · Game

Play: Fiber Optic Relay

Bounce a light ray into a receiver, bend it from air into water, then trap it inside a glass fiber and decode a four-bit pulse train. The angle at the boundary is the whole story.
